extracted.intended_audience: law professors, federal judges, appellate practitioners, and advanced law students interested in standing, remedies, and public-law litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of doctrines and litigation practices for challenging executive or administrative enforcement measures (standing doctrines, multi‑party suits, and remedial tools such as nationwide injunctions). Useful for scholars and litigators framing and evaluating suits against executive enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing Broad Pecuniary Injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: States are often in a position to assert financial (pecuniary) injuries because they govern, employ people, maintain large budgets, and enter public‑private agreements; courts have found such pecuniary harms meet Article III standing requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include lost revenue for regulatory programs, increased costs of providing government services, costs incurred as an employer, and financial harms to public universities. The Texas DAPA driver’s‑license loss example (projected multi‑million dollar losses) was accepted as a sufficient Article III injury; the government’s "self‑inflicted" argument was rejected when it would impinge on state sovereignty. See Texas v. United States; City of San Francisco v. Trump; Nevada v. U.S. Dep’t of Labor; Washington v. Trump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing New Sovereign Injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts recognize a broad spectrum of injuries to state sovereignty or quasi‑sovereignty that are more political than private‑law harms and can support standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These include harms to a state's ability to protect the environment or enforce its environmental laws (Massachusetts v. EPA), impairments to recruiting/retaining National Guard members that affect territorial protection, and injuries to a state's ability to choose how to govern and regulate. Such sovereign injuries may be framed as impairing territorial or regulatory interests rather than purely pecuniary loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abdication Standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory that states should have standing when the federal government 'abdicates' enforcement in an area of exclusive federal jurisdiction — i.e., automatic state standing where the federal government abandons enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulated in the DAPA litigation (Texas v. United States) as a novel harm; the district court described the DAPA policy as a 'textbook' example if abdication standing were recognized. Courts have signaled interest in such theories but have not definitively endorsed or rejected them; they may remain available as creative theories for future cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice Without Standing (Parties Without Standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a court finds that at least one plaintiff has standing, it commonly stops probing standing for every joined plaintiff; parties that lack individually confirmed standing often remain in the case and effectively participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: (1) entrenches current doctrine because courts need not confront novel theories, yet leaves those theories alive for future cases; (2) allows multiple plaintiffs to participate informally, bringing resources, institutional imprimatur, and expertise to the suit. Examples: California v. Trump (only some states found to have standing but others not dismissed); Texas DAPA (only Texas had standing but other states remained). See critique in Bruhl, One Good Plaintiff Is Not Enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augmenting Congress's Voice Through Amicus Participation
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress cannot be a formal party, courts often afford Congress a particular receptive posture as amicus — sometimes providing argument time and citing congressional amicus briefs — thereby giving Congress a voice in separation‑of‑powers litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House Counsel not only files briefs but frequently is given argument time; courts vary in responsiveness to amici but often cite congressional briefs. This participation lets Congress influence litigation over executive enforcement even where it lacks party status. See examples where Representatives’ briefs were cited and the rising trend of the House participating as amicus since 2019.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationwide Injunctions Tailored to Enforcement Lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts increasingly employ nationwide injunctions as a remedial response to executive or administrative enforcement actions, using these injunctions to bar enforcement broadly (often against executive branch actions rather than statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern nationwide injunctions have been used against executive orders, enforcement memoranda, and agency rulemaking (travel bans, DACA rescission, sanctuary‑cities policies, DOL overtime regs, 'public charge' rule, etc.). Historically more common in recent administrations; district courts have issued these remedies frequently and across many judges, making them a fixture of contemporary remedial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Enforcement Lawmaking from Congressional Legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts treat enforcement‑oriented executive actions differently from acts of Congress, often more willing to enjoin executive enforcement measures than to invalidate statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in sanctuary‑cities litigation: district courts issued nationwide injunctions against an Executive Order or agency conditions but upheld statutory requirements where Congress had acted. Judicial readiness to restrain enforcement lawmaking is higher than willingness to enjoin or alter congressional legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudential Limits on Injunction Scope (including injunctions against the President)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts may issue sweeping remedies, they exercise prudential restraint regarding the scope of injunctions — particularly injunctions that would directly bind or enjoin the President personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have declined to enjoin the President personally as an extraordinary measure (County of Santa Clara v. Trump; El Paso County briefing on scope), reasoning that the President may have no individual role in carrying out the challenged executive action. Judges consider percolation, conflicting obligations, and public repercussions when shaping injunction scope, and often tailor remedies to avoid extraordinary intrusions while still restraining unlawful executive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and Doctrinal Debate Over Legitimacy of Nationwide Injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an ongoing scholarly debate about whether nationwide injunctions are consistent with Article III's case‑or‑controversy limits versus having foundations in equitable tradition and historical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some scholars argue nationwide injunctions exceed Article III and should be limited to party‑specific relief (dispute‑resolution model); others (e.g., Sohoni, Frost, Siddique) locate historical practice and equity traditions supporting broader remedial power and treat scope as a prudential question. The Article brackets the jurisdictional-source debate and focuses on why courts resort to the remedy in enforcement litigation.
